slides.title: Number Systems
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. Today we revisit the family of numbers — natural, whole, integer, rational — and discover the rule that decides when a fraction has a terminating decimal expansion. Pace yourself across the lesson; target 5 minutes per concept slide and 8 minutes on the decimal rule.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Recognise N, W, Z and Q and the inclusion N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q.
Express any rational number in standard (lowest) form.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rationals confidently.
Decide whether a rational has a terminating or recurring decimal from its denominator alone.
Convert recurring decimals to p/q form.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective and ask students to flag the one they feel least sure about. Use that signal to weight the lesson.

slides.title: Natural, Whole and Integer Numbers
bullets: Each set extends the previous one to enable a new operation.
0 is whole but not natural; negatives are integers but not whole.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress the why: N → W lets us 'count nothing'; W → Z lets us subtract a larger from a smaller. Tie each extension to a real-life motivator (temperatures below zero, debts).

slides.title: Rational Numbers
bullets: A rational number is p/q with p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0.
Equivalent rationals: p/q = (kp)/(kq) for any non-zero k.
Rationals are dense — between any two there are infinitely many.
slides.speaker_notes: Pause on density: ask students to find any rational between 1/2 and 1/3 — this surfaces the LCM-of-denominators trick used later.

slides.title: Comparing rationals
bullets: Always check both denominators are positive before cross-multiplying.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk slowly through the cross-multiplication trick, then show the LCM check side-by-side so students see both methods give the same answer.

slides.title: Operations on rationals
bullets: Add / subtract: rewrite with common denominator (LCM is efficient).
Q is closed under +, −, ×, and ÷ by non-zero rationals.
Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.
slides.speaker_notes: Highlight the 'flip and multiply' rule; many students mis-apply it. Reinforce that division by 0 is the one operation Q is not closed under.

slides.title: Worked example: simplify (3/4 + 1/6) ÷ (5/12 − 1/4)
slides.speaker_notes: Move through each step at the board so students see the LCM choice, the reduction, and the 'flip and multiply' move all in context.

slides.title: The decimal-expansion rule
bullets: Every rational has a decimal expansion that is terminating or recurring.
p/q in lowest terms: factorise q.
Any other prime factor → recurring decimal.
slides.speaker_notes: This is the most powerful idea in the chapter. Long-divide 7/40 and 5/12 live so students see the rule confirmed.

slides.title: Recurring → fraction: convert 0.4̄5̄ (bar over 45)
slides.speaker_notes: Generalise: for an n-digit repeating block, multiply by 10^n. If there's a non-repeating tail, multiply by an extra factor of 10 first.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 3. Decide whether 11/64 has a terminating decimal.
Compare answers with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Look for students who are computing instead of factorising for question 3 — the rule is meant to bypass long division.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q2. Is the set of integers closed under division?
Q4. What property is used in 2/3 + 1/4 = 1/4 + 2/3?
Show your answers on fingers (1 = first option, 2 = second...).
slides.speaker_notes: Use the show-of-fingers tactic to gauge the room without singling anyone out. Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q — each extension closes a new operation.
Rational = p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0; standard form needs HCF = 1, q > 0.
Q is closed under +, −, ×, and ÷ by non-zero.
Decimal terminates iff lowest-terms denominator is 2^m × 5^n.
Recurring → fraction: multiply by 10^(block length), subtract, solve.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 5 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce the homework prompt.
